Chapter 8: Curiosity, Compassion, and the Questions That Never End
If there’s one thing the mortician discovered, it’s that curiosity doesn’t really disappear. Even adults—who’ve learned to tuck their questions away behind polite nods and quiet smiles—still find themselves wondering about the details no one talks about.
The thing is, the mortician made it her personal mission to answer every question, no matter how odd, awkward, or even a little uncomfortable.
Picture this: one evening, there’s a group of friends gathered around for what they call a “death dinner.” The whole idea? Anything goes—ask what you’re really wondering about mortality. The questions fly. Someone’s curious, “What happens if somebody dies in space?” Another person, a little quieter, asks, “How do you cope with seeing so much grief every day?”
The mortician took each question in stride. Sometimes she’d answer with a story, sometimes with a gentle laugh that made everyone relax. And it became obvious—when people are given permission to ask, they’re actually hungry for real understanding.
There were tender moments, too. One woman, who had recently lost her husband, softly asked if it was normal to talk to his ashes. The mortician reassured her, letting her know that grief takes all sorts of shapes, and those small rituals—no matter how unusual—can really bring comfort.
Another man, feeling anxious about his own mortality, asked what it’s like to be around death every single day. The mortician admitted it could be tough, but she added that it was grounding, too. “It reminds me to live fully,” she said.
And then there’s the honesty that only kids bring. At a school assembly, a little boy asked, “Are ghosts real?” The mortician smiled and told him she’d never seen a ghost herself, but she believed our memories can stick around in places and people long after someone’s gone. The children seemed happy with that answer, nodding knowingly.
Most of us don’t realize just how much comfort can come from a simple, honest conversation. The mortician noticed that when people felt safe enough to ask their questions, their fears lost some of their sharpness.
Curiosity, when met with compassion, became a bridge—connecting the living and the dead, the things we know, and everything we don’t.
The questions never really stop. But with every answer, the mortician found that the world felt a little less scary…and a whole lot more full of wonder.
